topic: Peter Safar invented CPR but couldn't save his own daughter, then built the first paramedic ambulance service.
title: CPR's Inventor Couldn't Save His Own Daughter With It
description: Peter Safar invented modern CPR in 1960, but in 1966 he couldn't save his own 11-year-old daughter from a severe asthma attack. Instead of stopping, his grief helped launch the first paramedic ambulance service in America. AI-narrated commentary on the human cost behind a medical breakthrough most people take for granted.

hook_candidates.text: Peter Safar, who invented CPR, still couldn't save his own daughter.
Could the man who invented CPR actually save his own daughter with it?
Inventing CPR didn't guarantee Peter Safar could save his own family.
In 1966, Peter Safar got the call every parent dreads, already knowing CPR.

share_trigger: A viewer sends this to the friend who took a CPR class once and assumes it always guarantees a save, because they want to show even its own inventor couldn't guarantee that.
contradicted_belief: Most people assume the person who invented CPR could always use it to save the people he loved most.
closing_comment: Wild that CPR's own inventor couldn't save his daughter, but saved thousands through the paramedics he built after.

sources.note: Confirms Safar developed modern CPR and that his daughter Elizabeth died in 1966 despite his resuscitation attempt.
Confirms Safar helped found the Freedom House Ambulance paramedic service in Pittsburgh.

beats.text: Peter Safar, who invented CPR yet **couldn't save** his own daughter.
beats.broll_query: a man in a white lab coat standing motionless in a dim 1960s hospital corridor, single overhead light

beats.text: Before 1960, there was **no standard way** to restart a stopped heart.
beats.broll_query: a black-and-white 1950s hospital ward with doctors standing helpless around a still patient on a gurney

beats.text: He combined his own mouth-to-mouth research with chest-compression trials to create the **ABC sequence** taught worldwide.
beats.broll_query: two 1960s doctors demonstrating chest compressions and mouth-to-mouth breathing on a resuscitation training mannequin under clinical light
a chalkboard with the letters A B C written huge in white chalk, dust drifting in spotlight

beats.text: A year after his daughter's funeral, Safar helped build one of America's **first paramedic** ambulances.
beats.broll_query: a boxy 1960s ambulance parked outside a brick rowhouse at dusk, its back doors open, warm streetlight

beats.text: In 1967, Freedom House in Pittsburgh trained ordinary citizens, not doctors, to run **emergency care**.
beats.broll_query: a group of ordinary men in plain jackets practicing bandaging on each other in a 1960s community hall
a man in a flannel shirt confidently pointing at a stethoscope on a hook, warm kitchen light

beats.text: Though a few **other cities** were racing toward the same idea.
beats.broll_query: a worn 1960s United States map on a wall with pins in several different cities, warm desk lamp

beats.text: But in 1966, his own **11-year-old daughter** Elizabeth had a severe asthma attack.
beats.broll_query: a child's bedroom at night, an inhaler on the nightstand beside a single dim lamp, empty bed

beats.text: He restarted her heart and lungs, but her **brain** had already gone too long without oxygen.
beats.broll_query: a heart rate monitor screen showing a faint returning pulse, sterile blue hospital light, close on the display
